artifacts.title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint by an ordained Deacon whose nomination for re-election was not advanced by the Session, holding that the Session's exercise of discretion in evaluating a candidate's eligibility for office did not constitute clear error requiring reversal. The dissent argued the proper standard of review was BCO 39-3.4 (de novo for constitutional interpretation), not 39-3.3 (great deference), because the Session applied extra-biblical and extra-constitutional attendance standards in blocking re-election.

artifacts.title: Dunn and Pesnell v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: TE Dunn and TE Pesnell complained that Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery erred in adopting its commission's recommendation to institute process and proceed to trial against TE David Swavely for alleged pastoral and spiritual abuse. The SJC denied the complaint, finding that the Presbytery had sufficient authority to proceed to trial and that the errors alleged did not rise to a reversible level.

artifacts.title: Sawyers et al. v. Missouri Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Complainants alleged Missouri Presbytery erred in failing to find a strong presumption of guilt that TE Jeffrey Meyers held views contrary to the Westminster Standards in its BCO 31-2 investigation. The SJC found that MOP erred but declared the case moot because MOP had already conducted a trial of TE Meyers during the pendency of the case before the SJC.

artifacts.title: Bordwine v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: TE James Bordwine and others challenged Pacific Northwest Presbytery's handling of study reports on TE Peter Leithart's Federal Vision-related teachings and its refusal to declare those views either orthodox or out of accord with the Standards without judicial process. The SJC sustained the complaint, held that presbytery erred in declaring the views not out of accord, and remanded for pastoral counsel or BCO 31-2 action; concurring and dissenting opinions were recorded.
